name: Breaking the Chain: The Fight to End Slavery
description: From the Atlantic trade to the last abolitions: the enslaved rebels, campaigners, writers and lawmakers who ended legal slavery across the Atlantic world, and how it is remembered.

checkpoints.name: A trade in people
checkpoints.note: From the early sixteenth century ships carried millions of enslaved Africans across the Atlantic to grow sugar. Dahomey and the Ashanti Empire sold captives, a king of Kongo protested to Portugal in vain, and firms such as the Royal African Company profited. The Quakers were among the first to condemn slavery, and Olaudah Equiano's life story of 1789 moved British readers.

checkpoints.name: Revolt and law
checkpoints.note: Enslaved people in Saint-Domingue rose in 1791. Toussaint Louverture led the revolution until the French seized him in 1802, and Jean-Jacques Dessalines declared Haiti independent in 1804. In Britain William Wilberforce led the campaign that banned the slave trade in 1807, the Slavery Abolition Act followed in 1833, and in the United States cotton spread slavery west.

checkpoints.name: Voices of freedom
checkpoints.note: Frederick Douglass, who had escaped slavery, became a leading speaker and writer. Sojourner Truth spoke for abolition and for women's rights, and Harriet Tubman led others north to freedom. Uncle Tom's Cabin reached a wide public in 1852 and made slavery the question American politics could not avoid.

checkpoints.name: Emancipation in America
checkpoints.note: During the American Civil War, Abraham Lincoln's Emancipation Proclamation of 1863 declared enslaved people in rebel areas free, Harriet Tubman guided a Union raid that freed hundreds, and the Thirteenth Amendment ended slavery throughout the United States in 1865.

checkpoints.name: Late endings and memory
checkpoints.note: The Empire of Brazil ended slavery in 1888, the last country in the Americas to do so, the year before its monarchy fell. In 1948 the Universal Declaration of Human Rights said that no one shall be held in slavery. The 1977 miniseries Roots and the novels of Toni Morrison brought the history of slavery before millions.
